title: What actually keeps customers with your business at 100k
hook: What actually keeps a customer with a business near 100k is the history that customer has built inside what they bought from you.
caption:
What actually keeps a customer with a business near 100k.

It comes down to the history they have built inside what they bought from you, far more than any line on the feature list and more than the price you charge them.

Six months of their own history inside the product. A way of using it that fits their week. A teammate they brought in on their own. A third tool that now talks to yours automatically.

A customer who has all four of those built up is not leaving next quarter, even when a cheaper option shows up in their inbox. A customer who has none of them is one email away from trying something else.

A business near 100k will often spend the week trying to add one more feature, when the same week could be spent making the customer's investment stick.

Three questions to ask yourself this month about your top customers.

One. On day thirty, what does a good customer have inside the product that they did not have on day one?

Two. On day ninety, what have they set up that would take a full working day to rebuild somewhere else?

Three. On day one hundred eighty, who else have they brought in from their own team or their own workflow?

Thin answers mean a thin customer. Specific answers mean the customer is yours.

title: What actually keeps a customer at a business near 100k
hook: What keeps a customer with a business near 100k is rarely what the team thinks it is. It is the history that customer has built inside what they bought from you.
tweets:
What keeps a customer with a business near 100k is rarely what the team thinks it is.

It comes down to the history the customer has built inside what they bought from you, far more than the feature list or the price.

Thread on how to protect that history, and what happens when it is left unprotected.

A customer on day thirty has almost nothing to lose by leaving, while a customer on day one hundred eighty has built a full week around using you, brought a teammate in, and taught three other tools to talk to yours automatically.

Those two customers look identical on a revenue report, and they behave nothing alike when a cheaper option shows up.

There are five things that hold a customer in place at month six.

Their own data inside the product, a habit that lives on a specific weekday, a teammate who also uses it, a tool it now connects to, and a saved template or view that only makes sense to them.

Score your top twenty customers against those five. One point each, with a maximum of five per customer.

A business near 100k will often find its top twenty average around two, which points to a design problem rather than a loyalty problem. The product was never built to ask the customer to put anything down inside it.

What moves the score up looks small on the surface.

Small templates the customer names themselves. A second user invited by the first. A third tool that now writes into yours automatically. A weekly step the customer has started doing on a specific day.

What does not move the score up is most of what ends up on the roadmap.

A better landing page, a louder email, a new feature the competition will ship next week anyway, a discount, a webinar, a push notification the customer did not ask for.

The same design that holds customers also pulls in the kind of customer worth holding on to.

A product that expects investment sorts out the casual buyer before they ever pay, and you stop paying to acquire people who were never going to stay long enough to matter.

Which of the five is weakest in your business right now? Reply with a number one to five, or the word none if you cannot tell yet.

title: How to tell if your product has real retention pull
hook: The customer who stays a year is rarely the one who had the best first impression. It is the one who built a habit inside what you sold them.
caption:

title: 5 questions that tell you if a customer will actually stick
hook: 5 questions that tell you how hard it would be for your customer to walk away from your business this quarter.
caption:
5 questions that tell you how hard it would be for your customer to walk away this quarter.

One. Can they take everything they made with you, in a single click, on the day they decide to leave?

Two. How many working hours would it take for that customer to rebuild their current setup somewhere else?

Three. Are they working alone, or did they bring a teammate in to use it alongside them?

Four. How many other tools now talk to yours automatically for that customer?

Five. What would that customer actually lose on the day they cancelled?

Score the top twenty customers in your business out of five. If the average lands below two, the product is not asking the customer to invest anything yet, which is where retention actually lives.

caption:
The real retention work at a business near 100k is about protecting what the customer has built inside what they bought from you, not what you keep adding on top of it.

Six months of their own history, a workflow they trained in on their own time, a teammate they pulled in, a habit that lives on a Tuesday afternoon. That is what makes a customer stay, far more than any line on the feature list.

title: How to Use Meta Ad Library Like a Creative Strategist
hook: The Meta Ad Library works as the fastest research tool a creative strategist has, provided you stop using it as a hook-farm and start using it as a research tool.
caption:
How to use the Meta Ad Library as a creative strategist.

The Ad Library works as the fastest research tool a creative strategist has, provided you stop using it as a hook-farm. When people grab a first line from a winning ad and paste it into their own ad, they wonder why it did not convert, and the answer is that the line was never the reason the ad was winning in the first place.

Here is the scan that actually works. Seven short steps, around twenty minutes.

One. Filter by the last ninety days and sort by start date, because the ads running right now are the ads worth looking at and the dead ones only tell you what stopped working months ago.

Two. Look at the age of every ad you find. An ad that has been live for more than sixty days is almost certainly working, because the brand would have killed it otherwise, and you should write those brand names down on one page.

Three. Look across versions inside the same brand. A brand running four variants of the same ad is testing, and the variant still running after three weeks is the winner, which is your data point rather than a random screenshot.

Four. Pull the angle underneath the hook, not the hook itself. The hook is the delivery, while the angle is the actual argument the ad is making about the product and the buyer. Write that argument down in one sentence.

Five. Note the mechanism the ad uses to make the claim believable, such as a face on camera, a before and after, a stat, a named system, or a customer testimonial. Name it on the page.

Six. Note the offer, not the words around it. A trial, a bundle, a one-time price, a subscription with a floor. The offer moves an ad more than the hook will, and it belongs on the page beside the angle.

Seven. Note what is missing across all of the winning ads. The angle nobody in the category is running, the channel nobody is trying, the promise nobody is making. That gap is where your own ad goes.

Run ten ads through those seven steps on one Sunday and you will walk into your next call able to answer what the brand should test next, rather than quoting what a course taught you last year.

title: What to note from every winning ad
hook: Five things worth writing on one page for every winning ad you save, so your swipe folder turns into a strategy document inside a month.
caption:
What to note from every winning ad.

There are five things worth writing on one page for every ad you save, and they turn the folder into a strategy document inside a month.

The angle is what the ad is arguing underneath the hook, not how the line is phrased on the surface.

The mechanism is the reason the ad says it works, whether that is a named system, a habit, or a claim about how the product changes the outcome.

The proof is the evidence the ad gives the viewer, such as a face on camera, a stat, a before and after, or a customer testimonial.

The call to action is what the ad is asking the viewer to actually do next, written as the literal step they take.

The emotional frame is what the ad is leaning on, whether that is relief, aspiration, curiosity, or urgency, named in one word.

Organize your swipe by angle rather than by creator. Inside a month you will have a strategy document, and the prospect on your next call will see the difference immediately.
